title: Companion standards: from primitives to implementations
scope: This collection links the archive’s algorithm profiles to the surrounding specifications: modes, parameters, key formats, protocol profiles, selection lists and validation records. It preserves particular editions and their dates rather than claiming to hold every standard or the latest version of every document.

An algorithm release, a national-standard issue, an effective date, an RFC publication and a product certificate describe different events. A protocol profile can expose exact mathematical and wire-format choices while leaving deployment and implementation approval unresolved.

The original files remain unchanged. Documented statements have source locators; deductions identify their premises and assumptions. Acquisition failures and incomplete copies are listed alongside successful preservation.

The 2026-10-20 continuation adds Russian national-language modes and correction records, complete-body Chinese companion scans, Japanese and Korean protocol records, German ECC/Brainpool material, French ANSSI guides, international mobile specifications, and Swiss/Swedish historical records. The original 2010 SM2/SM3 releases remain the earlier preserved editions.

layers.name: Primitive
layers.question: What mathematical transformation is specified?
layers.examples: SM2 point arithmetic; SM3 compression; Magma and Kuznyechik block transformations.

layers.name: Mode and parameters
layers.question: How are messages, nonces, tags, curves and keys selected?
layers.examples: GCM, CCM, CMAC, MGM; concrete SM2 and GOST curve parameters.

layers.name: API and encoding
layers.question: How does software represent and invoke the operation?
layers.examples: PKCS #11 objects and mechanisms; X.509 identifiers, public keys and signatures.

layers.name: Protocol profile
layers.question: How do peers negotiate and combine the parts?
layers.examples: TLS, IPsec/IKEv2, SRTP, and cellular EEA3/EIA3.

layers.name: Selection and policy
layers.question: Which algorithms and lifetimes does a dated policy recommend?
layers.examples: CRYPTREC list categories and BSI TR-02102 recommendations.

layers.name: Implementation evaluation
layers.question: What evidence concerns a particular implementation or evaluation?
layers.examples: Known-answer tests, design evaluation reports, and separately dated product certificates.

families.name: Common modes, formats and Suite A interfaces
families.reading_order: Read the primitive or mechanism interface, then the mode definition, then the protocol that uses it. The PKCS #11 Base and Historical Mechanisms copies deliberately share the v3.0 publication date.
families.boundary: A public API can constrain roles, sizes and representation without publishing a classified round function. Generic NIST modes do not establish NSA approval of a named Suite A algorithm.

findings.text: SP 800-38A specifies ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR confidentiality modes; SP 800-38D specifies GCM and GMAC and requires a 128-bit block cipher for GCM.
CMAC supplies message authentication, CCM combines counter-mode encryption with CBC-MAC, and SP 800-38F specifies methods for cryptographic key wrapping. These documents address distinct operations.

The preserved PKCS #11 Base and Historical Mechanisms specifications are both OASIS v3.0 standards dated 2020-06-15. The base API and historical mechanism descriptions are separate companion documents.

RFC 5280 profiles X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists; RFC 8446 specifies TLS 1.3. Their publication category is Standards Track, which is distinct from the Informational categories of several national-algorithm profiles.

If a product uses MEDLEY with GCM exactly as defined in SP 800-38D, the block cipher supplied to that mode has 128-bit blocks. This deduction supplies neither its key length nor its round construction.
findings.assumption: The manufacturer’s GCM label refers to the standard mode without a proprietary change in its block interface.

findings.text: HKDF separates extraction of a pseudorandom key from expansion of output keying material. PKCS #5 v2.1 separately specifies PBKDF2, PBES2 and PBMAC1 for password-based derivation, encryption and authentication.

The preserved RFC index supplies stream, publication-status and current-status fields. For example it labels RFC 2994 Legacy, RFC 5528 IETF and Informational, and RFC 5529 IETF and Proposed Standard. The category printed in each RFC and the index’s more specific status remain distinct fields.

families.name: Russia: GOST parameters, modes and protocol bindings
families.reading_order: Start with the Russian modes text, official registration record, separate 2018 correction and per-key data-volume recommendation. Then choose the algorithm generation, parameter/KDF documents, certificate or PFX encoding, and the required TLS/IPsec/CMS profile. RFC 9337’s integer-counter notation is an explicit unresolved compatibility question.
families.boundary: The preserved GOST binding RFCs are Informational Independent Submissions. RFC 8645 is an IRTF Informational document. These distinct streams do not imply IETF standards-track endorsement or establish the original Russian approval dates. The Russian printing and separate erratum are reproduced by a mirror with advertising-link text; they are not authenticated publisher downloads. RFC publication category varies across generations.

findings.text: RFC 4357 provides additional modes, key meshing, wrapping, parameter sets and identifiers for the older GOST algorithm family. RFC 7836 adds HMAC, VKO key agreement, KDF and wrapping constructions and elliptic-curve parameters for the 2012 family.
MGM is an authenticated-encryption mode defined for both 64-bit and 128-bit block ciphers. RFC 9058 supplies test vectors for Kuznyechik and Magma.

source_refs.locator: Abstract; Section 4; Appendices A.1 and A.2

findings.text: RFC 9227 binds Magma and Kuznyechik in MGM, with external rekeying, to ESP and IKEv2. RFC 9189 profiles GOST for TLS 1.2; RFC 9367 separately defines cipher suites, signature schemes and key exchange for TLS 1.3.
RFC 9215 specifies GOST signature/hash identifiers, parameters and encodings for the Internet X.509 PKI, including public-key encoding and signature representation.
RFCs 7836, 9058, 9189, 9215, 9227 and 9367 are Informational Independent Submissions. RFC 8645 is Informational in the IRTF stream and describes symmetric rekeying mechanisms.

source_refs.locator: Header; Abstract; Status of This Memo

findings.text: An implementation described only as supporting GOST is underspecified: interoperation also requires agreement on the primitive generation, curve or parameter set, mode, rekeying rules, encoding and protocol profile.
findings.assumption: The parties exchange keys, signatures or protected messages using the cited protocol families.

findings.text: GOST R 34.13-2015 cites approval order 750-st of 2015-06-19 and an effective date of 2016-01-01. The acquired Russian printing has a 2016 cover and an imprint signed for printing on 2016-03-28; these are separate milestones.

source_refs.locator: Foreword, PDF p.2; printed p.1 / PDF p.6; imprint, PDF p.29
Registration in the fund: order number, order date and effective date

findings.text: The Russian modes standard defines ECB, CTR, OFB, CBC, CFB and MAC procedures and supplies examples for 128-bit and 64-bit block ciphers. Its Magma CBC example uses a 192-bit initialization register for a 64-bit block cipher.

source_refs.locator: Sections 5.1–5.6; Appendix A; A.2.4.1, printed p.21 / PDF p.26

findings.text: The separately preserved IUS No.6/2018 correction changes Section 5.3.2, rule (7), of GOST R 34.13-2015. It is retained as a correction document, without altering the earlier printing’s acquired bytes.

source_refs.locator: Entire one-page correction, location column and corrected formula

findings.text: R 1323565.1.005-2017 addresses permissible plaintext-block volumes processed under one key for certain GOST modes. It cites approval on 2017-10-25 and states effective 2018-04-01. Its scope assumes the adversary cannot obtain additional information about the key.

source_refs.locator: Foreword, PDF p.2; Introduction, PDF p.4; Section 1, printed p.1 / PDF p.5

findings.text: RFCs 4490 and 4491 were issued as Standards Track in May 2006 and bind the older GOST signature/hash family to CMS and X.509 respectively. RFC 9215 is a separate 2022 profile for the 2012 signature/hash algorithms; the editions are not interchangeable.

RFC 9337 specifies password-based derivation with HMAC using the 512-bit GOST R 34.11-2012 hash output, plus PBES2, PBMAC1 and ASN.1 identifiers. RFC 9548 separately profiles PKCS #12 PFX containers, private-key representations and certificates for GOST R 34.10-2012. Both are Informational Independent Submissions.

There is a visible counter-encoding discrepancy between the preserved texts: RFC 8018 Section 5.2 defines INT(i) as four octets with the most significant octet first, while RFC 9337 Section 3 defines Int(i) using i=i1+2^8*i2+2^16*i3+2^24*i4 and Section 4 uses S || INT(i). This is recorded as a specification question, not a verified implementation failure or a completed errata audit.

source_refs.locator: Section 3, Table 1 Int(i); Section 4, U_1(i) equation

findings.text: An IV length alone cannot identify the cipher’s block size: the preserved GOST example explicitly uses an initialization register longer than one block.
findings.assumption: The interface implements the cited GOST mode and its generalized register construction.

findings.text: Literal implementations of the two counter definitions require an explicit compatibility decision before assuming identical PBKDF2 outputs. No claim is made here about deployed implementations or the resolution of any erratum.
findings.assumption: The Int/INT notation in RFC 9337 denotes its tabulated integer encoding; no external correction or implementation-specific convention overrides it.

families.name: China: original releases, parameters and successive standards
families.reading_order: Read the original 2010 release and curve sheet, then the acquired 2012 application/message/certificate/token standards and historical 2014 SSL VPN specification. S109 fills the missing GM/T 0009 body pages. Compare each with its exact later revision and the separate RFC 8998 TLS 1.3 profile.
families.boundary: The new Chinese scans are third-party mirror copies, not authenticated publisher downloads. S109 supplies the full 2012 application body, while S074 remains incomplete. The 2023 revision announcement still does not supply full revised texts. The 2012/2014 companion editions and the RFC’s TLS profile remain separate.

findings.text: The Chinese authority’s announcements No.21 and No.22 are dated 2010-12-17 and release SM2 and SM3 respectively. Their attached official algorithm PDFs carry December 2010 covers.

source_refs.locator: Release date and announcement text; attachment links
Release date and announcement text; attachment link

findings.text: The 93-page SM2 release combines Parts 1–4: general elliptic-curve rules, signatures, key exchange and public-key encryption. A separate one-page official attachment recommends a 256-bit prime-field curve and gives p, a, b, n, Gx and Gy.

source_refs.locator: Part covers at PDF pages 1, 47, 61 and 80

findings.text: The recommended SM2 curve has p = FFFFFFFE FFFFFFFF FFFFFFFF FFFFFFFF FFFFFFFF 00000000 FFFFFFFF FFFFFFFF and a = p − 3. Its equation is y² = x³ + ax + b over that prime field. This parameter choice is more specific than the general label elliptic-curve cryptography.

source_refs.locator: Curve equation and parameter lines p and a

findings.text: The original SM3 specification uses 512-bit message blocks, 32-bit words, 64 compression rounds, modular addition, XOR, rotations and Boolean functions, and outputs 256 bits.

The 2012-11-22 announcement lists GM/T 0009-2012 for SM2 applications, GM/T 0010-2012 for signed/enveloped message syntax, GM/T 0014-2012 for certificate-authentication protocols and GM/T 0015-2012 for certificate format.

Announcement No.45, posted 2023-12-23, lists 2023 revisions of GM/T 0009, 0010, 0014 and 0015 among other standards and states an effective date of 2024-06-01. The web posting date is recorded separately from each standard’s issue date.

source_refs.locator: Posting date; announcement; attached standards list

findings.text: The official GB/T records for SM2 Part 1 and SM4 record issue on 2016-08-29 and implementation on 2017-03-01. These are later national-standard milestones, separate from the 2010 SM2 release and 2012 industry-standard announcements.

RFC 8998 profiles SM2, SM3 and SM4 for TLS 1.3, including SM4-GCM and SM4-CCM cipher suites. It is an Informational Independent Submission, while the underlying TLS 1.3 specification RFC 8446 is Standards Track.

The curve sheet and SM3 text allow concrete descriptions of arithmetic, parameters and hashing without inferring those choices from a codeword. The published record does not, by itself, identify the original classified design date or every government use.
findings.assumption: The question concerns the preserved public specifications and their dated releases, rather than an undocumented earlier variant.

findings.text: A second GM/T 0009-2012 acquisition contains 12 PDF pages, including all printed body pages 1–7. Its cover prints issue and implementation on 2012-11-22; its final imprint says first edition and printing in January 2013. The older S074 remains a separately preserved incomplete scan.

source_refs.locator: Cover; contents; printed body pp.1–7 / PDF pp.5–11; imprint / PDF p.12

findings.text: GM/T 0009-2012 specifies private/public-key and encryption/signature data formats. Its public-key BIT STRING contains 04 || X || Y, with 256-bit coordinates. Its encryption structure lists XCoordinate, YCoordinate, a 32-byte hash and ciphertext; its signature representation contains integer R and S fields.

source_refs.locator: Sections 5.1–5.2 and 7.1–7.3, printed pp.1–3 / PDF pp.5–7

findings.text: The application standard defines identity preprocessing and, absent a special agreement, the 16-byte user identity represented by the ASCII string 1234567812345678. RFC 8998 instead specifies a TLS-specific SM2 signature identity for its handshake context and separately discusses certificate identities.

source_refs.locator: Section 8, printed p.4 / PDF p.8; Section 10, printed p.7 / PDF p.11
Section 3.2.1, SM2 signature scheme identity values

findings.text: GM/T 0010-2012 defines object identifiers and signed, enveloped, signed-and-enveloped, encrypted and key-agreement message structures, with SM2 key syntax in normative Appendix A. These are message encodings around the primitive.

source_refs.locator: Section 5; Sections 8–12; normative Appendix A, printed p.9 / PDF p.12

findings.text: GM/T 0014-2012 specifies certificate-system protocols and associated message formats; Section 5 refers SM2 key structures to GM/T 0009 and encapsulation to GM/T 0010. GM/T 0015-2012 separately specifies DER-based certificate and CRL structures and encoding examples.

source_refs.locator: Section 5, printed p.2 / PDF p.7; Section 6; Appendices A–B

findings.text: GM/T 0017-2012 is a smart-token interface data-format specification whose Sections 7–9 cover command/response APDUs, instruction/status-byte encoding and commands. The scan’s cover prints the 2012 edition and 2012-11-22 issue/effective dates.

source_refs.locator: Cover, PDF p.1; contents, PDF pp.2–5; Sections 7–9

findings.text: The acquired GM/T 0024-2014 is an SSL VPN specification with issue and effective dates 2014-02-13 on its cover. It is a historical Chinese VPN specification, separate from the 2021 RFC 8998 TLS 1.3 profile.

source_refs.locator: Cover, PDF p.1; contents and Scope

findings.text: Interoperation requires agreement on identity preprocessing, point/ciphertext/signature representation and the protocol binding. The label SM2 support alone leaves choices visible in these companion documents unresolved.
findings.assumption: The implementations exchange the specified SM2 objects or signatures, rather than merely using elliptic-curve arithmetic internally.

families.name: China and 3GPP: ZUC, EEA3 and EIA3
families.reading_order: Read ZUC Document 2 for the keystream generator, Document 1 for the EEA3/EIA3 packet algorithms, Document 3 for implementer test data and Document 4 for design/evaluation history. The Release 19 ETSI wrapper records the later standards context.
families.boundary: These copies come from different dated editions; they are not a single synchronized conformance package. In particular, the Release 19 wrapper specifically references Document 1 v1.7, whereas the separately preserved Document 1 is v1.8. Test vectors and design evaluation are separate kinds of evidence.

findings.text: The archive holds ZUC Document 2 v1.6 (2011-06-28), EEA3/EIA3 Document 1 v1.8 (2019-01-24), Implementor’s Test Data v1.1 (2011-01-04), and Design and Evaluation Report v2.0 (2011-09-09).

The EEA3/EIA3 document history records initial publication on 2010-06-18, an EIA3 modification on 2011-01-04, and maximum-message-length changes in 2011 and 2019. The design report records the first public release of that report on 2010-08-11 and a ZUC/EIA3 modification in January 2011.
The test-data preface includes internal ZUC state and input/output examples, but expressly says conformance with the test data does not guarantee a correct implementation.

ETSI TS 135 221 v19.0.0 is dated October 2025 and identifies 3GPP TS 35.221 Release 19. Its technical provisions are incorporated by reference to EEA3/EIA3 Document 1 v1.7; the separately archived Document 1 is v1.8.

The name ZUC alone does not fully specify the cellular confidentiality or integrity operation: EEA3 and EIA3 define different uses of the generator, with packet inputs and initialization rules. Version history is necessary when interpreting early analyses.
findings.assumption: The implementation or historical analysis concerns the 128-EEA3/128-EIA3 family covered by these records.

families.name: Japan: selection lists, additional primitives and Camellia profiles
families.reading_order: Compare dated CRYPTREC selections with the primitive specification. Camellia’s mode/test-vector, IPsec and TLS documents have different RFC categories. MISTY1, KCipher-2 and KASUMI are separately specified primitives; a later RFC or standards wrapper does not date their invention.
families.boundary: CRYPTREC list membership and category are dated policy evidence. They do not establish first invention, implementation certification or universal government approval.

findings.text: The preserved legacy CRYPTREC list is dated 2003-02-20 and includes a 2005-10-12 correction appendix. The archive also holds the 2013-03-01 list and the list revised 2026-03-30, whose family cover date is 2023-03-30.
The March 2026 list places Camellia among e-Government Recommended Ciphers and CLEFIA among Candidate Recommended Ciphers. A separate Monitored Ciphers category also exists.

source_refs.locator: e-Government Recommended, Candidate Recommended and Monitored tables; PDF pages 1, 4 and 5

findings.text: The strength-requirements PDF’s revision table records first publication on 2022-07-01 and corrections on 2023-03-30. Its cover still states March 2022; the archive retains that internal date discrepancy.

source_refs.locator: Cover; revision table in introductory pages

findings.text: RFC 5932 specifies Camellia cipher suites for TLS (June 2010), and RFC 4312 specifies Camellia for IPsec (December 2005). Both were published with the Standards Track category.
A claim that Camellia and CLEFIA have the same CRYPTREC recommendation status loses a distinction visible in the preserved 2026 list. An accurate claim names both the edition and category.
findings.assumption: The claim refers to the March 2026 CRYPTREC list, rather than a different selection program or edition.

findings.text: RFC 5528 gives Camellia CTR/CCM algorithms and test vectors; RFC 5529 binds CBC/CTR/CCM to IPsec. Both date to April 2009, but the first is IETF Informational and the second Standards Track. RFC 6367 adds Camellia TLS cipher suites in September 2011 as IETF Informational.

source_refs.locator: RFC5528, RFC5529 and RFC6367 stream/status entries

findings.text: The new primitive records include MISTY1 (RFC 2994, November 2000), KCipher-2 (RFC 7008, August 2013) and an April 2022 Release 17 KASUMI specification. These are concrete preserved editions, not common first-approval dates.

The December 2002 3GPP TR 55.919 design/evaluation report explicitly describes KASUMI’s changes from MISTY1 in the data-encryption part and key schedule. Its cover marks the preserved copy as not approved by the Organizational Partners and not for implementation; its design history is not an approval record.

families.name: Republic of Korea: SEED and ARIA protocol profiles
families.reading_order: Use the existing SEED and ARIA primitive specifications, then the TLS and IPsec/SRTP bindings as relevant. The KCMVP programme pages are acquisition leads only until their original bytes can be preserved.
families.boundary: The three KISA pages returned HTTP 503 and were not preserved. No current KCMVP eligibility list, complete validation procedure, or certificate is asserted from those unavailable pages.

findings.text: RFCs 4162 and 4196 bind SEED to TLS and IPsec, with publication dates August and October 2005. Their preserved headers give the Standards Track category.

RFC 6209 defines ARIA cipher suites for TLS (April 2011). RFC 8269 defines ARIA for SRTP (October 2017), including CTR/GCM, key derivation, DTLS-SRTP profiles and MIKEY parameters. Both are IETF Informational documents.

source_refs.locator: Header; Abstract; Status of This Memo
Header; Abstract; Status of This Memo

findings.text: The protocol records establish specified interoperability choices, but they do not by themselves show that a named product passed Korean module validation. Such a claim needs a product-specific validation record and its scope.
findings.assumption: The proposed claim concerns implementation validation rather than publication of a protocol profile.

findings.text: RFC 4010, issued Standards Track in February 2005, specifies SEED in CMS and supplies identifiers for its use. It is an encoding/protocol companion rather than a module-validation certificate.
RFC 5669, issued IETF Standards Track in August 2010, specifies SEED for SRTP/SRTCP, including CTR, CCM and GCM, nonce formats, SEED-CTR key derivation and test vectors.

families.name: Germany: ECC constructions, Brainpool and protocol guidance
families.reading_order: Read TR-03111 for concrete signature/key-agreement operations and encodings, RFC 5639 for Brainpool parameters and RFC 8734 for its TLS 1.3 binding. TR-02102 supplies the separately dated recommendation and protocol context.
families.boundary: General BSI technical guidance is not a public specification of LIBELLE or proof that a particular SINA product is approved for a classification level. It also does not establish CHIASMUS’s internal construction.

findings.text: The archived TR-02102-1 is version 2026-01, as of 2026-01-23. It provides general cryptographic mechanism and key-length recommendations.
TR-02102 Parts 2, 3 and 4 address TLS, IPsec/IKEv2 and SSH respectively. Each preserved edition’s history dates version 2026-01 to 2026-01-27.

The TR series supplies a public policy and protocol context for German deployments; identifying the mathematics or approval scope of an opaque product still requires a record that names that product and its algorithm or certification boundary.
findings.assumption: No additional product-specific approval or algorithm specification is supplied by the generic guidance citation.

findings.text: BSI TR-03111’s cover and history identify version 2.10 dated 2018-06-01 and its initial public version on 2007-02-14. The URL filename’s V-2-1 token is not the printed version number.

source_refs.locator: Cover, PDF p.1; History, PDF p.2

findings.text: TR-03111 separately specifies ECDSA, ECGDSA, EC Schnorr signatures, elliptic-curve key agreement, derivation functions and PACE, then gives public-key/signature input-output formats and OIDs.

RFC 5639 supplies Brainpool curve parameters and generation procedures. RFC 8734 separately specifies Brainpool groups and signature schemes for TLS 1.3. Both are Informational Independent Submissions; a curve definition and a TLS binding are different records.

families.name: France: ANSSI selection and mechanism rules
families.reading_order: Read the distribution-page snapshot, then the exact cover and history of each guide. The rules PDF is version 3.00 of March 2026; the selection guide is version 1.0 of March 2021. Use cited specifications for the actual algorithm and encoding.
families.boundary: A distribution page’s date does not redetermine a linked PDF’s edition. Recommendation, reference-rule compliance and product certification remain different attributes. The earlier v2.04 PDF was not recovered in this pass.

findings.text: The current ANSSI distribution page is dated 2026-03-20 and links two guides. The mechanisms rules PDF is version 3.00 dated 2026-03-20; the algorithm-selection PDF remains the initial version 1.0 dated 2021-03-08.

source_refs.locator: Publication date and two download links

findings.text: The mechanisms guide’s revision history records a first applicable version on 2004-11-19, v2.04 on 2020-01-01 and v3.00 on 2026-03-20, with the quantum threat added to the latter. These are guide-version milestones.

The 2021 selection guide separately recommends key-wrapping mechanisms SIV and AES-KeyWrap, KDFs including HKDF and PBKDF2, and selected elliptic-curve families including Brainpool. Recommendations are attached to specified mechanisms and implementation notes.

source_refs.locator: Sections 4.6–4.8, printed pp.26–28 / PDF pp.28–30; Section 5.3, printed pp.31–32 / PDF pp.33–34

findings.text: The 2026 rules guide recommends seeking post-quantum security for mechanisms expected to remain in use after 2030-01-01 or exposed to retrospective decryption risk. The guide states that general rule compliance alone is insufficient to guarantee mechanism security.

source_refs.locator: Section 2, RecoSécuLongTerme, printed p.8 / PDF p.10; Section 1.4, printed p.5 / PDF p.7

findings.text: The two currently linked guides must be interpreted with their own dates and scopes. A 2026 webpage does not establish a 2026 revision of every recommendation in the 2021 PDF.
findings.assumption: The historical question concerns the acquired PDF editions, not an unpreserved later revision.

families.name: International mobile standards: SNOW 3G, UEA2 and UIA2
families.reading_order: Read Document 2 for the generator, Document 1 for packet confidentiality/integrity, Document 3 for tests and Document 5 for design history. The GSMA distribution index records the provenance of these copies.
families.boundary: The preserved companion documents have different dates and version numbers. The historical evaluation describes its contemporary design rationale; it is not a present-day security guarantee. This is an international standardization context, not a national approval inventory.

findings.text: SNOW 3G Document 2 v1.1 is dated 2006-09-06 and records initial publication on 2006-01-10. The generator uses a 128-bit key and 128-bit initialization variable, a 16-word LFSR and a three-register FSM, with 32-bit output words.

source_refs.locator: Cover; Document History, PDF p.2; Sections 2.1, 3.2 and 3.3

findings.text: UEA2/UIA2 Document 1 v2.1 is dated 2009-03-16. Its confidentiality and integrity algorithms use distinct input mappings and generator uses; the history identifies the 2009 change as a C-code improvement.

source_refs.locator: Cover; Document History, PDF p.2; Sections 3–4

findings.text: The design/evaluation report describes SNOW 3G as a modification of SNOW 2.0 and explains changes to the FSM and nonlinear components. Its v1.1 cover is dated 2006-09-06; its history records v1.0 on 2006-02-06.

source_refs.locator: Cover; Document History, PDF p.2; Sections 8.1.2–8.3

findings.text: The implementors’ test document is v1.1 dated 2012-10-25, distinct from the 2006 primitive and design documents and 2009 packet specification. GSMA’s distribution page links these records and states its distribution role for UEA2/UIA2.

source_refs.locator: UEA2 & UIA2 distribution section and Documents 1–5 links

findings.text: A name such as SNOW 3G identifies a generator; a complete cellular operation also needs the confidentiality or integrity construction, initialization mapping, length conventions and exact companion edition.
findings.assumption: The target implementation follows the preserved UEA2/UIA2 family, rather than another use of the underlying generator.

families.name: Swiss and Swedish historical machine records
families.reading_order: Start with the original bilingual NEMA instructions and their cover stamp. For Siemens T52, separate FRA’s retrospective institutional history from Borelius’s explicitly hypothetical reconstruction of Beurling’s working method.
families.boundary: The manual’s original issue date is unverified. Borelius’s account was written in the 1980s and is not Beurling’s contemporaneous laboratory record. Raw web snapshots do not include every externally linked image.

findings.text: The NEMA instructions’ cover identifies copy 717 and bears a declassification stamp dated 1992-07-09. The bilingual German/French instructions are preserved as 18 PDF pages of scanned booklet spreads; the original publication date is not established.

source_refs.locator: Cover, PDF p.1; German opening, PDF p.2; French portion

findings.text: FRA’s official history identifies the G-schreiber as Siemens und Halske T52 and dates the first interception of the relevant teleprinter traffic to 19 May 1940. It separately dates FRA’s establishment as an independent agency to 1942-07-01.

source_refs.locator: G-skrivaren, printed pp.8–9 / PDF p.5; FRA bildas, printed pp.10–11 / PDF p.6

findings.text: FRA identifies Carl-Gösta Borelius as a participant in G-schreiber cryptanalysis from 1941 and describes this account as written in the 1980s. Its introduction explicitly presents a reconstruction of how Beurling may have proceeded, rather than a disclosed account by Beurling himself.

source_refs.locator: Introduction under Hur gjorde Arne Beurling för att forcera G-skrivaren?; concluding paragraphs

findings.text: The 1992 declassification stamp dates release of a secrecy control on the surviving manual; it supplies no first-use or first-approval date for the NEMA machine.
findings.assumption: The stamp is read as a declassification annotation on this copy, without an additional original approval record.

limitations.title: Incomplete application-standard scan
limitations.text: S074 remains the original three-page incomplete booklet scan and must still be labeled incomplete. S109 is a separate 12-page mirror acquisition whose complete body sequence 1–7 has been checked against the contents. The earlier gap is filled for the 2012 application text; the old bytes are retained for provenance. This does not supply the 2023 revision.

limitations.title: Korean validation acquisition gaps
limitations.text: S084, S085 and S099 each returned HTTP 503 again on 2026-10-20 after one respectful retry. Prior errors remain in acquisition_history. No current KCMVP eligibility list, procedure page or product certificate is claimed. New SEED RFC companions do not resolve this gap.

limitations.title: Revised standards announced but not fully acquired
limitations.text: S073 preserves the official announcement and list of 2023 industry-standard revisions. The archive does not claim to contain the full text of every listed revision. Historical 2012 material cannot silently substitute for a 2023 edition.

limitations.title: Translations and mutable publisher URLs
limitations.text: The earlier Alipay-hosted English SM2/SM3/SM4 files remain separately labeled translations with edition uncertainties. The newly acquired official Chinese release files supply independent 2010 evidence. BSI and CRYPTREC URLs may later change their contents; SHA-256 and acquisition times identify the copies used here.

limitations.title: Status and coverage limits
limitations.text: RFC categories and streams describe publication status at issue. This guide does not perform a complete present-day obsolescence, errata or approval audit. Full ISO/IEC standards and every national standard cited by the profiles are not all preserved. Historical rotor-machine records remain in their existing profiles; modern companion standards are not retroactively applied to Enigma, Lorenz or Fialka.

limitations.title: Mirrors, overlays and incomplete authentication
limitations.text: The Chinese scans are pinned to a third-party GitHub commit and retain scan marks. The Russian Meganorm copies include host-added advertising-link text. Their acquired bytes are unchanged, but neither host is the original issuing authority. Rosstandart’s independently preserved catalogue record confirms the identified modes standard and dates, not the byte authenticity of every mirrored page.

limitations.title: French historical guide recovery and edition mismatch
limitations.text: The former v2.04 mechanisms-PDF URL now redirects to a current distribution page. The archive acquired the linked March 2026 v3.00 rules and March 2021 v1.0 selection guide separately. The historical v2.04 file and RGS key-management Annex B2 were not acquired; attempted B2 locations returned 404. data/acquisition-attempts.json records these outcomes.

limitations.title: GOST password-KDF notation remains a specification question
limitations.text: The literal integer-counter encodings in RFC 8018 and RFC 9337 differ. The guide records the equations and their locators, without silently merging the definitions, asserting a deployed failure, or claiming that all errata and implementations have been audited.
